title: When do you choose interface vs abstract class — and why does Java 8+ blurring (default methods) still not make them interchangeable?
shortTitle: When to choose interface vs abstract class — Java 8 default methods still don't make them interchangeable

s1_definition.profdef: Choose INTERFACE when: defining a capability/contract that UNRELATED classes can implement (Auditable, Comparable, Serializable), need multiple inheritance of type (class implements 5 interfaces), or the contract has no mutable state. Choose ABSTRACT CLASS when: sharing mutable STATE (fields) and CONSTRUCTORS among a family of RELATED classes (SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount share balance, accountId), or need non-public methods (protected helper methods). Java 8 default methods narrowed the gap — interfaces can now have method bodies. BUT they are NOT interchangeable because: (1) interfaces CANNOT have constructors, (2) interfaces CANNOT have instance fields (only public static final constants), (3) interface default methods are implicitly public (no protected/private pre-Java 9), (4) a class can extend only ONE abstract class but implement MANY interfaces. These four differences still drive the choice.
s1_definition.analogy: Interface = a banking LICENSE ("you MUST provide deposit() and withdraw()") — any institution (bank, fintech, cooperative) can hold it. Multiple licenses allowed. Abstract class = a BANK TEMPLATE with pre-filled forms and a vault (state) — only branches of THIS bank can use it. You can only belong to ONE bank (single inheritance) but hold many licenses (multiple interfaces). Java 8 gave licenses the ability to include instructions (default methods) — but licenses STILL can't have a vault (state) or a reception desk (constructor).
s1_definition.oneliner: Interface: capability, multiple inheritance, no state. Abstract class: family, shared state, constructors. Java 8 default methods: still no constructors, no instance fields, no protected methods on interfaces. Choose based on: need state? → abstract. Need multiple? → interface.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Choose INTERFACE when: defining a capability/contract that UNRELATED classes can implement (Auditable, Comparable, Serializable), need multiple inheritance of type (class implements 5 interfaces), or the contract has no mutable state. Choose ABSTRACT CLASS when: sharing mutable STATE (fields) and CONSTRUCTORS among a family of RELATED classes (SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount share balance, accountId), or need non-public methods (protected helper methods). Java 8 default methods narrowed the gap — interfaces can now have method bodies. BUT they are NOT interchangeable because: (1) interfaces CANNOT have constructors, (2) interfaces CANNOT have instance fields (only public static final constants), (3) interface default methods are implicitly public (no protected/private pre-Java 9), (4) a class can extend only ONE abstract class but implement MANY interfaces. These four differences still drive the choice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Interface = a banking LICENSE ("you MUST provide deposit() and withdraw()") — any institution (bank, fintech, cooperative) can hold it. Multiple licenses allowed. Abstract class = a BANK TEMPLATE with pre-filled forms and a vault (state) — only branches of THIS bank can use it. You can only belong to ONE bank (single inheritance) but hold many licenses (multiple interfaces). Java 8 gave licenses the ability to include instructions (default methods) — but licenses STILL can't have a vault (state) or a reception desk (constructor).

**One line to remember:** Interface: capability, multiple inheritance, no state. Abstract class: family, shared state, constructors. Java 8 default methods: still no constructors, no instance fields, no protected methods on interfaces. Choose based on: need state? → abstract. Need multiple? → interface.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — A developer tried to use an interface with default methods to replace the Account abstract class.** Failed because: (1) couldn't add balance field (interfaces have no instance fields), (2) couldn't add constructor to initialize accountId (interfaces have no constructors), (3) couldn't make validate() protected (interface methods are public). The developer switched back to abstract class for Account and used interfaces for cross-cutting capabilities (Auditable, Taxable).

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Account needs: accountId field, balance field, constructor, protected validatePositive(). ALL of these require abstract class — interface can't provide any of them.

**Step 2.** Auditable and Taxable are capabilities — any class (Account, Trade, Invoice) might need them. Multiple inheritance needed. MUST be interfaces.

**Step 3.** Account implements BOTH interfaces + extends nothing but is abstract itself. SavingsAccount extends Account → gets: state (balance), constructor, protected methods, AND both capabilities (Auditable + Taxable).

**Step 4.** Java 8 default methods let Auditable provide `auditSummary()` with a body. But Auditable STILL can't have a balance field or a constructor. The four differences remain.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ JAVA 8 BLURRING — BUT STILL NOT INTERCHANGEABLE ═══

  BEFORE Java 8:
    Interface: abstract methods ONLY
    Abstract class: abstract + concrete methods + state + constructors

  AFTER Java 8:
    Interface: abstract + DEFAULT methods + static + private (J9)
    Abstract class: same as before

  STILL DIFFERENT:
    Feature              │ Interface          │ Abstract Class
    ─────────────────────│────────────────────│──────────────
    Instance fields      │ ❌ NO              │ ✅ YES
    Constructors         │ ❌ NO              │ ✅ YES
    Protected methods    │ ❌ NO (pre-J9)     │ ✅ YES
    Multiple inheritance │ ✅ YES             │ ❌ NO (single)
    Default methods      │ ✅ YES (Java 8)    │ ✅ YES (always had)

  ═══ DECISION FLOWCHART ═══

  Need instance fields? ──YES──→ ABSTRACT CLASS
  Need constructors? ────YES──→ ABSTRACT CLASS
  Need multiple types? ──YES──→ INTERFACE
  Unrelated classes? ────YES──→ INTERFACE
  When in doubt? ────────────→ INTERFACE (default)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Choose interface when defining a capability that unrelated classes can implement (Auditable, Comparable, Serializable) — multiple inheritance of type. Choose abstract class when sharing mutable state (balance field, auditLog list) and constructors among a family of related classes (SavingsAccount IS-A Account). Java 8 default methods narrowed the gap by adding method bodies to interfaces — but they are STILL not interchangeable.

The four remaining differences: interfaces cannot have instance fields (only public static final constants), cannot have constructors (no state initialization), default methods are implicitly public (no protected access for family-only methods), and a class can extend only ONE abstract class but implement unlimited interfaces. In my Account hierarchy: Account is an abstract class (has balance, accountId, constructor, protected validatePositive). Auditable and Taxable are interfaces (cross-cutting capabilities any class can have). Account implements BOTH — best of both worlds.

The modern guideline: default to interface. Use abstract class ONLY when you need constructors or shared mutable instance fields. In Spring Boot: services implement interfaces (loose coupling, multiple implementations). JPA entity base classes are abstract classes (shared @Id, @CreatedDate fields, constructor initialization). The choice is driven by STATE — if you need shared mutable state with initialization, abstract class. If you need a contract with optional default behavior, interface.
